📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Premier League is set to introduce a newly introduced LGBTQ+ inclusion campaign after ending its partnership with Stonewall, the charity behind the widely recognised Rainbow Laces initiative.

Stonewallâs Rainbow Laces campaign, released in 2013, became a fixture across English football, with players from all Premier League clubs wearing rainbow-coloured laces and captains donning rainbow armbands to promote acceptance and equality. The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences.".

Despite Stonewall's efforts, recent reports from Kick It Out reveal an alarming increase in discriminatory incidents in football, including rises in sexism, transphobia and faith-based abuse, with racism continuing to be the most prevalent issue.

Sources indicate that controversies around playersâ attitudes to rainbow armbands have also made headlines. Last season, Ipswich captain Sam Morsy declined to wear one due to religious beliefs, while Crystal Palaceâs Marc GuÃ©hi faced criticism for personalising his armband with the phrase âI Love Jesus.â.

Additionally, Manchester United scrapped prepares for LGBTQ+ support jackets after a player refused to participate.

With no openly gay or bisexual players currently in the Premier League, and the surge in discriminatory incidents, some question the timing of the split from Stonewall â an organisation highly respected for its work in LGBTQ+ advocacy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) manufacturer.
  • The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.
  • The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) manufacturer.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It noted in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

According to recent reports, "The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company stated Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The manufacturer's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he stated.

It has been revealed that "His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research manufacturer Radio Free Mobile, noted the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the manufacturer is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Sources indicate that huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

Industry observers note that however, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

It has been revealed that however, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

In a recent development, the US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Sources indicate that windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the manufacturer. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he noted.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion organization in October 2025.

In a recent development, however, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

The most likely time for Bastoni to walk away from San Siro was last summer, when he was still stinging from a series of controversies including his red card in the World Cup play-off against Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Since then, he has won the Scudetto and Coppa Italia Double at Inter, and restored some of his reputation for Italy.

Hundreds of millions of people around the world are affected by diabetes mellitus1. It develops when the activity of insulin, a glucose-lowering hormone secreted by pancreatic β-cells, becomes insufficient to maintain healthy glucose levels in the blood. The condition can be managed with oral medication or by injecting insulin and other metabolic hormones, but the constant need for people with diabetes to manage their lifestyle and blood-glucose levels can impair their quality of life. Therapeutic approaches that monitor and control blood glucose automatically are therefore highly desirable. Writing in Nature, Xiu et al.2 report proof of principle of a bioelectronic device called NeuroAxis that does exactly that in rat models of diabetes.

Recent findings suggest that for the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

In a recent development, spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur.

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

In a recent development, “I am really aware of the situation,” Sage mentioned. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”.

In a recent development, the decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

Sources indicate that it was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

Recent findings suggest that “Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We revealed our maturity. We are improving.”.

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. Maybe we could score more goals with more nastiness, but I am very happy because we created many chances. We need more goals for sure. It’s not enough, but we are improving a lot.

“I was very nervous before the game, during the game, after the red card, it’s always better playing with one player more. But today, against this team, they played with this behaviour, all behind the line of the ball, aggressive. Very tough game.”.

When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”.

Recent findings suggest that speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.

“The main message was don’t concede again, stay tight as a defence and try to hit them on the counter. That is the best proposal when you’re down a man.

Sources indicate that “Unfortunately, it didn’t happen today. We know what we can do as a team, as a back five, the whole unit. There were some positives in the games, but I can’t say much when you lose. We just have to go again.

Sources indicate that “Hopefully, the next game we win. The main message is to stay together as a team. We know what we are capable of. It is staying confident and bouncing back.”.

This result, coupled with the 3-1 victory over Coventry City in their previous home outing, means that Tottenham have won back-to-back league games and are beginning to gather some momentum under Roberto De Zerbi.

In his pre-match press conference, when asked if he’s felt a change in atmosphere after the triumph at Stamford Bridge, De Zerbi replied: “We have not achieved our goal. To do that, we have to show if we are good enough. If we are good enough on the pitch, for sure we are ready. In the head, in the mentality, we have to show, because the step of this club is to win games in a row and to be angry day by day, game by game, win by win. One time or two times are not enough.”.

Palace have endured a tricky and inconsistent start to the season under their summer appointment Pierre Sage, accumulating just seven points from their opening seven league matches while shipping 17 goals. The 1-0 League Cup victory over Fulham in midweek has momentarily eased the pressure on the Frenchman, but given their newfound success in recent campaigns, fan expectations have risen, with recent performances prompting some cause for concern.

Tottenham remain without the suspended Rodrigo Bentancur, while Xavi Simons, Wilson Odobert, Lucas Bergvall, Savio, Tosin Adarabioyo and Mykhaylo Mudryk are out injured. James Maddison was substituted early in the second half at Chelsea with an apparent groin strain, but De Zerbi insists he’s available for this one. Destiny Udogie could also be involved after recovering from a knee problem.

The visitors are without the injured trio of Ismaila Sarr, Takehiro Tomiyasu and Chadi Riad, but there’s hope that Quinten Timber and Jorgen Strand Larsen are fit to be involved this evening after they both missed the Fulham victory.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with teams coming shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Antonio Conte reveals how his wife made pasta for John Terry and changed the course of his Chelsea career. ‘The club had no intention of renewing his contract, he wasn’t even mentioned.’.

The Italian tactician sat down with podcast Cronache di Spogliatoio and looked back over his long experience in Italy and England, including the Premier League title and FA Cup at Stamford Bridge from 2016 to 2018.

He explained that Terry’s playing career could’ve been so very different, as before he became a legend for the London club, he was about to be pushed out of the door.

“Terry was a fundamental figure in our Premier League title victory,” noted Conte.

Industry observers note that “A solid guy, he flew with a private jet along with his agent from London to see me in Turin. His contract was running down, he decided to pay for the flight to visit me.

Industry observers note that “He basically said I love Chelsea so much that I want to keep going. Until that day, we had never talked about Terry. Marina Abramovich said he wanted to come and talk to me, but they had no intention of renewing his contract.

Sources indicate that “My wife ended up making pasta for John Terry and his agent, who I had not met before. I assured him, I don’t care about how old you are, but if you prove that you deserve to play in training, then I will play you.

“The only promise you have to make is that even if you don’t play, you are still added value in the locker room, because you represent the history of this club.”.

At that time, Terry was 35 years old and Conte confirms Chelsea had not the slightest intention of keeping him in the squad, ready to let him leave as a free agent.

Industry observers note that “He simply wasn’t mentioned, that was the season when they finished 10th. I’d met all the Chelsea players a month earlier, but they didn’t let me meet Terry, because he just wasn’t on their radar,” added the coach.

Conte also reveals how Terry represented the Chelsea squad prompting a complaint for his very Italian way of working, which at the time seemed unusual to Premier League players.

Sources indicate that “Terry came to me in training one day and mentioned the players felt we were doing too much tactical work, too many videos. When my captain comes and tells me that, I have to speak to the staff and move towards them.

Industry observers note that “It might be a coincidence, but after that we drew with Swansea, lost to Arsenal, so I thought we’re going back to my approach. If we have to die, we die with my ideas,” insisted Conte.

According to recent reports, “The dressing room was bubbling up, ready to revolt, but then after another break, Terry comes to me. ‘Hey gaffer, we’ve got to keep doing the tactical stuff, because these things actually happened during the game!’.

“They realised he’s not just telling us things for no reason, they are situations you see in the match, and that changed everything,” concluded Conte.

#71768. Latest Update: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

Latest Update: 37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border.
  • Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
  • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

"November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

Industry observers note that "The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how swiftly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a upcoming one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people.".

According to recent reports, the people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home.".

In a recent development, today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

At the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very quickly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid.".

In a recent development, meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

It has been revealed that in his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid.".

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an concern that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

His photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Sources indicate that menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he noted.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened.".

It has been revealed that interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

In a recent development, the story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist remarked she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West.".

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she stated. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, remarked Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

"In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future.".

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," mentioned Feuchtenberger.

According to recent reports, "For me personally, the whole matter of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she said. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny.".

"This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," mentioned Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant.".

This article was originally written in German.

Why Everton School Visits Are Making A Mark

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Captain Underpants”. The laughter that follows is infectious. It seems doubtful that it was an honest answer to the question posed to Zach Lee by the young boy located somewhere near the front of the classroom: “What is your favourite book?” But it got exactly the reaction he was after.

The room is abuzz. It has been for much of the past hour.

According to recent reports, goalkeeper Lee and five of his Everton Under-21s teammates have gleefully taken up the task of being reading buddies to the children of Ellesmere Port’s Meadow Primary School, one of six schools that make up the recently renamed Everton Multi-Academy Trust (EMAT). Seven miles away, six of their Under-21 peers are doing likewise at Oldfield Primary School in Chester.

Nearer to Liverpool, the hollers that greeted Everton Women’s Holly McNamara and Karen Holmgaard 24 hours earlier are still reverberating around the corridors of Bidston Avenue Primary School.

Sources indicate that christian Nørgaard and close friends Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George are also familiar with the noise the pupils at the Birkenhead school can make. Last month, the trio were serenaded with a ukulele rendition of Spirit of the Blues on a visit there. Blue ukuleles, of course.

If the colour of the musical instruments is a cute indicator of the strengthening ties between the football club and the EMAT schools, the time being spared by the players is of much greater significance.

It is intended to demonstrate a cross-Club connection with EMAT, which sits alongside Everton in the Community as one of Everton’s associated organisations. “Part of the Everton family,” as Everton’s Chief Tax and Sustainability Officer and Chair of Trustees for EMAT Alison Haynes puts it.

But there is a deeper intention, too. “We want to use the power of the Everton crest to inspire and engage youngsters in education,” says Steven Baker OBE, CEO of EMAT. Baker has seen this in evidence for more than a decade, having previously served as Principal of Everton Alternative Provision Free School, the award-winning L4 facility that offers youngsters who have struggled in mainstream schools a route back into education.

It has been revealed that lee and his Under-21 colleagues, McNamara and Holmgaard are all supporting one particular mission of EMAT - to inspire youngsters towards a life-long love of reading. More immediately, to ensure they have the requisite literacy level to adequately prepare them for what lies ahead in secondary school education.

It has been revealed that in Ellesmere Port, Chester and Birkenhead, the players are tackling their role head on. Books - donated by Everton staff to help replenish the schools’ libraries - are strewn across the tables and spilling onto the floor. No-one’s troubled by the mess.

According to recent reports, julia Donaldson’s greatest hits are being played out across the room. Michael Morpurgo – a childhood favourite author of midfielder Jack Patterson – can be heard, too. ‘Bluey’ is an appropriately named hit on another table. And then there’s Lee and a group of little ones giggling at Captain Underpants.

Close by to the classroom at Meadow, Everton’s leading post-war goalscorer Graeme Sharp is here too, continuing the literacy theme by officially opening the school’s newly-refurbished library.

According to recent reports, “These children will remember today,” claims Baker. “They will remember players from Everton coming into school and taking the time to sit with them.

“They love hearing stories but they also love having someone to read to. Both aspects are so important for a child’s development.”.

As is music. It’s why Dibling, George and Norgaard found themselves being taught the chords to one of Goodison’s – and now Hill Dickinson Stadium’s – favourite tunes last month.

Studies show a direct correlation between a child mastering a musical instrument and making their mark in maths and other creative fields.

The Toffees trio left behind gifts of recorders (blue ones), helping the school expand the opportunities it can offer to its pupils.

“We find it’s really vital for their resilience and it's good for the children mentally and socially to have the opportunity to not only play an instrument, but to play to an audience,” says Bidston Avenue headteacher Stuart Brady, a Tranmere Rovers fan.

Recent findings suggest that “It's great for us as a school to have the connection we do with Everton and the players. Days like this are great, but it's also about the children feeling they belong to something bigger.”.

And the proof that EMAT is getting it right is stacking up. In 2024, Everton Free School and Everton Football College – the two original schools on which the Trust was founded – were jointly awarded an ‘Outstanding’ rating by Ofsted. Earlier this year, the respected national TES Awards named EMAT (then The People’s Learning Trust) as its Trust of the Year for trusts with nine schools or fewer.

With the support of a Premier League football club and its players behind them, it is hoped the collective will continue to go from strength to strength.

Recent findings suggest that the intention is that Everton’s Under-21s will return to the schools to resume their reading buddy duties at junctures throughout the season, strengthening their bonds with the schools and pupils. It is seen as a vital part of the players’ professional development.

Representatives from the Men’s and Women’s team will continue to play their part also. Merlin Röhl has already been a guest of Oldfield Primary School’s after-school chess club, taking up an invitation to share his love of the ancient game with the next generation.

It has been revealed that “We understand the responsibility and influence we have as a football club when it comes to our communities,” notes Haynes. “And you cannot understate the impact the player visits have.

“The atmosphere and the smiles you see in the room, the energy they give to the children… it’s truly wonderful.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that towards the end of their lives, stars experience a drastic change in their structure as they swell and enter what is known as their giant phase. Because most stars are thought to host orbiting companions (such as planets, other stars or black holes), interesting interactions can happen as the giant host expands. The most striking of these occur when a companion star is engulfed by a giant: astronomers refer to this as the common-envelope phase1. Despite theoretical expectations that common envelopes should be widespread in stellar evolution, they have been extraordinarily difficult to observe. Writing in Nature, however, Karambelkar et al.2 report the first direct detection of a star inside a giant star.

Norway's ice hockey team claims Russia replacing it at World Juniors

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant.
  • The move, which has yet to be publicly declared by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play.
  • The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association noted the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly declared by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF mentioned it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey.".

Recent findings suggest that as of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there.".

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days.".

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

Recent findings suggest that "However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place.".

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could problem visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications.".

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the problem could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

Recent findings suggest that some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

On April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning latest stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

It has been revealed that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling latest home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

This is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

Sources indicate that I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

Let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger issues and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

Not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

It has been revealed that inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

It has been revealed that if medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

Recent findings suggest that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

Industry observers note that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

It has been revealed that the club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

It is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too major for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

It’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

Oxford are hoping to move to a newly introduced stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

According to recent reports, 89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

Recent findings suggest that it was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

It has been revealed that walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the newly introduced ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

According to recent reports, 87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its concerns have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Recent findings suggest that it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the fresh-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

If you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two.

Not an awful lot to relish about the Broadfield Stadium, to be honest.

Decent fans, of course, just like at every club, but Crawley Town’s home is a bit of a modern monstrosity, next to a roundabout outside town on the A23.

Industry observers note that if you visit the Broadfield Stadium, I think you might doubt if Crawley are even in League Two. I had fun when I visited because I was in the away end with Stockport fans but I’m not in any hurry to go back.

85. Coventry Building Society Arena, Coventry City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2005 Capacity: 32,609.

Football at the CBS Arena feels like it is in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless.

When it was called the Ricoh Arena, I had no interest in visiting what is now the Coventry Building Society Arena because it felt like a symbol of the callous way in which fans of the club were being treated by SISU, the hedge fund that owned it at the time.

It has been revealed that but SISU sold up in the end and I went along a few years back to see Coventry dismantle Wayne Rooney’s Birmingham City. Then, in the press room beneath the stadium, I watched as my colleague Neil Moxley got into a decent old-fashioned row with Rooney about his stewardship of the Blues.

The atmosphere inside the ground was lively enough, partly because the game was a derby of sorts, but it is a soulless stadium abutting the M6.

It is football in an urban wasteland but it is football, nonetheless, and Doug King, the new owner, has brought with him much better times.

84. JobServe Community Stadium, Colchester United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2008 Capacity: 10,105.

This stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is rather a bleak place to watch football.

The staff at the club are great, the stewards are friendly, there's plenty of parking, there's a Wendy's next door and the home fans, largely arranged in a stand behind one of the goals, make a superb first of creating an atmosphere.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

It probably didn’t help that I went on a dank March night when a wispy fog lingered in the dim floodlight glare but there was something ethereally gloomy about the JobServe Community Stadium.

The empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

Home is home and there was still plenty of drama and passion in Colchester’s 1-0 victory over Chesterfield – the match I saw – but it came despite the stadium, not because of it.

According to recent reports, 83. Pallet-Track Bescot Stadium, Walsall.

Division: League Two Opened: 1990 Capacity: 10,863.

The Bescot Stadium was the first of the generation of identikit latest-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit fresh-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

It’s close to the M6 and it’s a seven-minute walk to Walsall station – so you can get away from it quickly, which some would say is a bonus.

82. Brick Community Stadium, Wigan Athletic.

Division: League One Opened: 1999 Capacity: 25,133.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

I stood on the terraces at Springfield Park as a Stockport fan.

Once again, it will not come as a surprise to learn I preferred it to its successor, the JJB Stadium, which later became the DW Stadium and is now the Brick Community Stadium.

The name changes are irrelevant to some but they betray a lack of care for the identity of a football club.

There were some great days and nights there when Wigan were promoted to the Premier League and I remember, in particular, the heady feeling of watching Wigan’s first home game in the top flight, against Jose Mourinho’s Chelsea in 2005.

The limelight has moved away again now and Wigan are left with a stadium that is perfectly adequate and also perfectly unremarkable.

It has been revealed that 81. The Croud Meadow, Shrewsbury Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 2007 Capacity: 9,875.

Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Gay Meadow, the former home of Shrewsbury Town, was one of the best grounds in our top four divisions.

It might have flooded now and again because of its position on the banks of the River Severn but it was a fine old ground and the tradition of a boatman taking to a coracle to fish wayward shots that cleared the roof of the stand out of the river was one of the most cherished peculiarities in our game.

Industry observers note that the Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

Recent findings suggest that 80. Select Car Leasing Stadium, Reading.

Division: League One Opened: 1998 Capacity: 24,376.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

And Wally took a swing at me at a Football Writers’ Association dinner a couple of years later.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Even if the Mad Stad doesn’t have an awful lot of personality, I have only respect for the Reading fans who endured so much under the ownership of Dai Yongge and fought for their club.

79. Pride Park Stadium, Derby County.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 32,956.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the new generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

This is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Pride Park is bland and featureless, a symbol of its team’s current struggle for identity as it languishes near the foot of the Championship.

Recent findings suggest that 78. Swansea.com Stadium, Swansea City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2003 Capacity: 20,996.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks character but is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

My in-laws used to live in Swansea and when I wasn’t out walking to Worm’s Head at Rhossili or enjoying the delights of Mumbles and the Wales Coast Path, I’d make the occasional pilgrimage to what was left of the Vetch Field.

Recent findings suggest that I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

I did a phone interview with Mike Tyson from the press box here a couple of hours before a game once. I couldn’t hear him very well because of various announcements being made over the loud-speaker system and soon, his tone became rather impatient but still, a conversation with Mike Tyson in the press box at Swansea is not easily forgotten.

Recent findings suggest that 77. Pirelli Stadium, Burton Albion.

Division: League One Opened: 2005 Capacity: 7,088.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

The main entrance of the Pirelli Stadium looks a little like a car showroom. The rest of it struggles for character, too.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

It has been a club to be admired for a long time, particularly under the former stewardship of Ben Robinson, who sold his majority stake to the Nordic Football Group.

They have punched above their weight for much of that time and their stadium is built for practicality, not for artistic merit.

Industry observers note that 76. Vitality Stadium, Bournemouth.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1910 Capacity: 11,307.

It’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

The club is one of the success stories of modern English football and the Vitality Stadium reflects its enthusiasm and, yes, vitality.

Industry observers note that it’s a bit of a Lego arena, sure, but it’s built for its audience and its catchment area. It’s a League Two stadium that got overtaken by the success of its side.

Its character comes from its small size and the atmosphere it generates because of it.

Abutting King’s Park and not far from the sea front, it’s a ground that almost manages to feel quaint. But not quite.

Sources indicate that 75. Club Doncaster Sports Village, Doncaster Rovers.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 15,148.

This is a uniform modern bowl on the outside of town rescued by the club’s excellent support.

It is, at least, a pleasant walk to the stadium on the outskirts of Doncaster.

I parked on the estate grouped around Lakeside Lake and strolled around its shores until I came to the stadium. Things go slightly downhill from there.

It’s a perfectly presentable stadium but there is little to distinguish it. It is a uniform modern bowl stuck on the outside of town that is rescued by the club’s excellent support.

74. St Mary's Stadium, Southampton.

Division: Championship Opened: 2001 Capacity: 32,384.

It doesn’t feel as though Southampton's St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of latest-builds largely devoid of character.

Southampton’s former ground, The Dell, was a wonderfully quirky stadium, full of odd tiers and shelves.

It doesn’t feel as though St Mary’s Stadium has any quirks, unfortunately.

Squatting at the edge of a slightly murky industrial estate, it falls squarely into the category of latest-builds largely devoid of character.

That does not mean that the home fans are incapable of creating atmosphere there and the renditions of When the Saints Go Marching In are a part of the cultural fabric of football in this country.

Sight lines are good and it can get loud but its design has little to recommend it.

Industry observers note that 73. King Power Stadium, Leicester City.

Division: League One Opened: 2002 Capacity: 32,259.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans can make plenty of noise but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the upcoming era of stadia.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the fresh generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

Division: League One Opened: 1961 Capacity: 7,426.

Broadhall Way is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere, and home to a friendly club.

Broadhall Way, now known as the SPORTA Arena, is a decent little ground with a good atmosphere.

And it is home to a fine club, one that has consistently achieved more than most expected of it and has held down its place in the Football League.

The Stevenage fans create more than their share of noise but it’s a friendly club with great staff and stewards.

It’s not spectacular but it’s a lovely day out watching football.

71. EV Charger Points Stadium, Cheltenham Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1927 Capacity: 6,923.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

Sources indicate that again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

It’s a shame because it’s a fine little ground that provides a different focus in a town dominated by horse racing.

70. LNER Community Stadium, York City.

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

According to recent reports, david 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he said of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The fresh stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our new high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

Sources indicate that I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The newly introduced stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Industry observers note that their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.

69. Priestfield Stadium, Gillingham.

Division: League Two Opened: 1893 Capacity: 11,582.

Some may damn Priestfield but Gillingham have played here for more than 100 years and that weight of history counts as much as anything when you visit a stadium.

However hard clubs may try to replicate tradition with forced rituals, you can’t cheat history.

Division: League One Opened: 1938 Capacity: 5,000.

It has been revealed that hayes Lane is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s still a pleasure to visit.

Hayes Lane – or the Copperjax Community Stadium, to give it its current name – is one of those stadiums that feels wide open to the elements. It’s the opposite of a tight, enclosed ground like Queens Park Rangers' Loftus Road but it’s still a pleasure to visit.

I went with Stockport when Bromley were in the National League and stood on the open terrace, which was reserved for away fans.

It was a wild evening in February 2022 and it felt as if the wind was blowing horizontal but County won 3-1 and a steward went out of his way to bring me a programme from where they were being sold in the home end, so it felt like a golden night all round.

Division: League Two Opened: 1978 Capacity: 5,032.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

The players who comprise the Class of 92 were the players at the heart of one of the greatest stories I ever covered – the Manchester United Treble of 1998-99 – so perhaps it shouldn’t be a surprise that I enjoyed my visit to Moor Lane, now rebranded as the AIG Stadium.

Many dislike and distrust the way Gary Neville, Ryan Giggs and the rest took over a non-League club and oversaw its rise to the Football League but I like what they’ve done at Salford.

It’s a neat little ground and it’s been nicely modernised without losing all its character.

66. One Call Stadium, Mansfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1861 Capacity: 9,376.

I didn’t know back when I first went that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest stadium in the league.

My only visit to Field Mill – now the One Call Stadium – was on Saturday, November 20, 1982.

I know this because I have always been a football stadium nerd and my 16-year-old self logged all the matches I went to in a King’s School Macclesfield exercise book.

I didn’t know then that Field Mill was, and is, the oldest continually used stadium in the league but I stood on an open terrace behind one of the goals that housed the away fans and watched Stockport lose 3-2 in an FA Cup first-round tie.

Recent findings suggest that maybe that was why I’ve never been back. The atmosphere was a little bit lost because it seemed so open but there is a stand now where that open terrace was. So maybe things have improved.

Division: Championship Opened: 1921 Capacity: 22,200.

I’ve always associated Watford's home at Vicarage Road with drama for some reason.

I’m going to show my age again: the first time I went to Vicarage Road, Graham Taylor was the manager, in his first spell at the club, and Ross Jenkins was playing up front in a match against Manchester United.

Maybe I’ve misremembered this but I seem to recall the train dropping us away fans right outside the stadium.

I’ve always associated Vicarage Road with drama for some reason. Even though it’s not tight and compact, it’s a place that can still generate a terrific atmosphere and I’ve seen a slew of upsets there.

The last one was when Liverpool visited in the middle of their runaway title-winning season in 2019-20.

They were still unbeaten in mid-February and on a long winning run and Watford took them apart and beat them 3-0. It was the kind of occasion that Vicarage Road excels at.

Everton’s upcoming ground is the latest to use its city’s waterway as a backdrop but the drawback to Middlesbrough’s home is its featureless interior.

It is a friendly, passionate place to watch a game but its design is unimaginative and bland.

Ground experiences are about a lot more than the game.

In a recent development, 61. Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff City.

Division: Championship Opened: 2009 Capacity: 33,280.

Cardiff's stadium may not be Ninian Park but it's still a good place to watch football because they are such a passionate group of supporters.

I was a journalism student in Cardiff so Ninian Park was the first ground where I ever sat in a press box. From that day to this, it’s never lost the thrill.

Rob Phillips, Cardiff’s South Wales Echo reporter at the time, was still commentating for the BBC until a few seasons ago. It is a handsome stadium on the inside but there have been times when I have visited when sections of it were shut down because of ticketing challenges.

Division: Championship Opened: 1887 Capacity: 27,000.

Ashton Gate is one of the stadiums that has slipped through the gaps for me.

I’ve only been once and that was for work but it’s a handsome stadium in a beautiful city with a rich history.

Owners are always threatening to move to a newly introduced site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.

A quirky mish-mash of a ground whose architecture betrays its origins as a rugby stadium, the Memorial Stadium is still a decent place to watch football.

I prefer the kind of visual chaos you get at this place – with the Popular Insulation Stand isolated like a widow stand on part of the one touchline, and the West Stand looking more like a cricket pavilion – than the monotonous uniformity you get at so many new-builds.

Owners are always threatening to move to a new site but the Memorial Stadium, successor to Eastville, still survives.

In a recent development, 56. BetWright Stadium, Leyton Orient.

Division: League One Opened: 1937 Capacity: 9,253.

In Orient’s case, they have still managed to retain the character and the pride of their famous old ground.

From the outside, the modern Brisbane Road looks as if it can’t make up its mind whether it’s a high-rise housing estate, a conference centre or a football ground.

It has been revealed that maybe that’s the point. Maybe the future for some clubs is to be all three.

In Orient’s case, they have still managed to retain the character and the pride of the famous old ground.

The East Stand, with the lovely old gable bearing the club’s name, is one of the best stands in the four divisions and, despite all the changes, the place oozes with the local character that makes the best football clubs so distinctive.

Recent findings suggest that I took my son to watch his first Stockport County game here when he was three. He didn’t catch the bug.

55. ProAmpac Stadium, Lincoln City.

Division: League One Opened: 1895 Capacity: 10,780.

It has been revealed that the English game is full of odd histories... and that's what makes it so utterly precious.

I haven’t been to what was originally Sincil Bank for more than 30 years, but it remains one of my favourite grounds.

The reason is that it’s the home of one of English football’s more eccentric traditions, the sounding of an air-raid siren every time Lincoln get a corner. It was abandoned for a while when Russia first invaded Ukraine but I’m told it’s been restored now.

The English game is full of odd histories. It’s what makes it so precious.

Division: League One Opened: 1888 Capacity: 23,287.

Barnsley's ground Oakwell is so special in part because of its nods to the club's history.

It has been revealed that they were heady days for Yorkshire football in the late 90s. Leeds United were in the Champions League and Barnsley spent a season in the Premier League.

Industry observers note that it was a treat to visit Oakwell in those days and watch Barnsley’s underdog story play out. But there’s another reason why a visit to Oakwell is still special.

The West Stand is one of few remaining examples in our league of a stand designed by the famous football architect Archibald Leitch and it is a thing of beauty.

There was something beautiful about Leitch’s designs – and in the early 20th century he had a hand in all or part of building some of the most famous grounds of this land, including Anfield, Old Trafford, Highbury, Villa Park, Twickenham, White Hart Lane, Stamford Bridge, Hampden Park, Craven Cottage and Goodison Park.

Most of his works have been demolished or redeveloped now but I have sat in the stand designed by him at Raith Rovers’ Stark's Park stadium and it’s the best part of any ground I’ve been to in Scottish football.

In a recent development, oakwell is precious because of that and because of other nods to the heritage of the club like the original changing rooms. Barnsley’s Premier League status came and went but the club have never lost their sense of history.

Industry observers note that 53. Ewood Park, Blackburn Rovers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1882 Capacity: 31,363.

Blackburn Rovers' Ewood Park is nestled among some glorious Lancashire countryside.

The first time I went to Ewood Park was October 1991 when I reported on the return of Kenny Dalglish to football management for Liverpool’s Daily Post.

I went a lot over the next 10 years as the good times rolled and it was a lovely opportunity to explore some of the Lancashire countryside around the town.

In a recent development, I loved it at Ewood Park. I liked being able to look out from the main stand at the gap between the stands opposite and see people standing on the hillside behind them, staring down into the stadium as the match unfolded.
