The days when Dalglish led them to a league title seem an awfully long time ago now.

52. AESSEAL Newly introduced York Stadium, Rotherham United.

Division: League Two Opened: 2012 Capacity: 12,088.

There’s something bold about Rotherham's New York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

There’s something bold about the Fresh York Stadium that elevates it above the standard new-builds.

The glamour of the name – a suburb of Rotherham, not just one of the greatest cities in the world – helps, as does the charisma and the vision of the chairman and owner, Tony Stewart.

It’s bold as brass and it carries it off.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2006 Capacity: 60,704.

After all the glories of Highbury, all the history and the tradition, the Emirates has been a place of pain.

If Arsenal were still at Highbury, it would be in my top five grounds.

Sources indicate that one of my best mates owns a flat in the Highbury apartment development, in the spot closest to where his season ticket was. It sends a shiver down my spine every time I go and visit. The respect Arsenal have shown to their old ground is a template for the way other stadiums should be preserved.

Sources indicate that there’s still a lot of class at Arsenal. Right from Lynne on the front desk at the Emirates to the people who work in the media department and the upper echelons of the club so, in that regard, it’s always a pleasure to visit.

Sources indicate that it hasn't happened much in the past few seasons, but the atmosphere turns poisonous here more quickly than any other stadium I know. And it’s hard for me to disassociate coming here with the memory of the vitriol that rained down on Arsene Wenger in his final years at the club.

The stadium is not as bland as some of the fresh generation but it still lacks real character and there is such a sense of entitlement and bitterness among the supporters that I have one friend, who is a season-ticket holder, who only goes to away games.

Industry observers note that 50. Weston Homes Stadium, Peterborough United.

Division: League One Opened: 1913 Capacity: 13,513.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road into a cauldron for major games.

I love London Road. Peterborough are a well-run club with a terrific owner in Darragh MacAnthony and a stadium that’s a fine mix of old and new, tradition and modernity.

This is a place with a proper identity and fans that make a lot of noise and turn London Road, or the Weston Homes Stadium, into a cauldron for substantial games.

It’s the kind of stadium where you can feel respect for the past as well as an embrace of the future.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 16,616.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love but any stadium where Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen once graced the turf should be a pilgrimage for any fan.

Bloomfield Road is in need of a little love these days but any stadium where stands bear the name of Stanley Matthews and Stan Mortensen, and where those two legends of the English game once graced the turf, should be a pilgrimage for any football fan.

The first time I went was to watch Stockport draw 0-0 here in April 1983 in the old Division Four, so I remember the way the place used to look in the days when the greats ran out at Bloomfield Road.

I was there in 2011, too, when Blackpool were back in the top flight, to see players like Charlie Adam and Marlon Harewood taking on Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United on a bitter January afternoon by the Irish Sea.

In a recent development, the stadium had changed by then and much of the character of the old ground was lost in the redevelopment. Those days in the top flight seem like a long time ago now but while they still play at Bloomfield Road, the echoes of history will make it a magical place.

Recent findings suggest that 48. Accu Stadium, Huddersfield Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1994 Capacity: 24,329.

According to recent reports, more stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

One of the best of the lower-division new-builds, the Accu Stadium is a classic of modern football architecture.

Nestled in the lee of a hillside, its elegant, striking architecture with its curved trusses makes it a worthy successor to the old Leeds Road ground.

In 2024, the Twentieth Century Society called for the stadium to be listed and named it one of the best upcoming buildings in the country in the last 30 years.

They’re absolutely right. More stadiums should be listed. More should have been protected. Too many have been lost but it’s not too late to safeguard the best of the ones that remain.

Recent findings suggest that 47. Adams Park, Wycombe Wanderers.

Division: League One Opened: 1990 Capacity: 9,558.

The stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight.

I know a lot of fans have Adams Park much lower on their list of stadiums to visit but I’ve always liked it.

Maybe it’s the bucolic setting, in the lee of a wooded hill on the edge of the Chilterns, that does it for me.

Recent findings suggest that the stadium might be modest but the team has a habit of punching above its weight. It’s a great place to go and feel the underdog spirit that is part of the force that drives English football.

Division: League Two Opened: 1878 Capacity: 9,507.

Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I'll still be calling it Spotland.

Industry observers note that the last (and only) time I went was on September 4, 1984, a Tuesday night for a League Cup first round match. The floodlights were dim but Spotland is a decent little ground in the middle of terraced streets that, I am told, has not lost its gritty character.

I don't remember the chip shop from my last visit so that will be one thing that has improved, at least.

Division: League One Opened: 1910 Capacity: 19,841.

Meadow Lane is a wonderful ground to visit and it's evolved into an impressive modern arena.

The first time I went to Meadow Lane, it was to see Manchester United play a top-flight game there.

Industry observers note that the away section was uncovered and the stadium had quirks and character. It’s still a wonderful ground to visit and it has evolved into an impressive modern arena that has plenty of nods to its rich history and its status as one of the founder members of the Football League.

Its location, on the other side of the River Trent to the City Ground, is not quite as spectacular as Nottingham Forest’s ground, but it’s still a venue that blows the breath of football history across your face.

Industry observers note that 44. Highbury Stadium, Fleetwood Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1939 Capacity: 5,137.

This Highbury may not be quite as august as Arsenal’s old stadium but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

Like Leeds, Morecambe and Grimsby Town, going to watch Fleetwood is enhanced by local fish and chips.

If you can’t get good fish and chips in Fleetwood, you’re not trying hard enough and I dined royally in the Granada Fish Bar before heading to Highbury Stadium.

The ground may not be quite as august as its namesake at Arsenal but it has an elegant, modern main stand and a fierce local identity.

Recent findings suggest that the club’s nickname is The Fishermen and the fans chant a lot about the Cod Army. It’s a great day out by the seaside.

Industry observers note that 43. University of Bradford Stadium, Bradford City.

Division: League One Opened: 1886 Capacity: 24,433.

Bradford's Valley Parade still has its character, and is a fine stadium to visit.

It is impossible to think of Valley Parade without thinking of the tragedy that befell Bradford City in 1985 when its main stand was engulfed by flames and 56 people lost their lives.

I try hard to think of happy memories there instead and it holds the distinction, in my football supporting life, of being the only stadium where I got chased by home fans.

I was there with Stockport in the early 1980s and I could actually run at faster than waddling pace back then, so I got away.

Valley Parade still has its character, it is still a fine stadium to visit. Every trip there is a chance to remember those who were lost.

Division: League Two Opened: 2013 Capacity: 6,500.

It has been revealed that the Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it. For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Hive flirts with soullessness but just about evades it.

For a start it’s one of the only stadiums that allows you to watch the action, fleetingly, from the London Underground.

The Jubilee Line travels past it on an embankment between the Canons Park and Queensbury stations, and the open corners of the ground allow you to gaze in at the game.

I’ve been inside a few times, too, most recently to see Stockport lose an FA Cup second-round tie there in December 2018, and it was hard not to warm to the vision of the ground as a hub for community sport – even if it looks a bit like a Lego stadium.

Recent findings suggest that 41. The Valley, Charlton Athletic.

Division: Championship Opened: 1919 Capacity: 27,111.

There is still something magical about The Valley, even if it has changed out of all recognition from its glory days.

The Valley has changed out of all recognition from the glory days when more than 75,000 crammed into it in the 1930s.

But there is still something magical about the home of Charlton Athletic. Perhaps, for those of us who are old enough, it is the memory of the old East Terrace rising up towards the south London sky. Even when it was crumbling and condemned, there was something majestic about it, something that recalled great days.

Perhaps, too, there is something about the knowledge of how hard the fans fought, for seven years in the late 80s and early 90s, to return to the stadium when it seemed it had been ripped away from them.

And even if only that memory of the old East Terrace remains now, the walk down into the valley where the revamped stadium nestles still feels like a journey to the heart of the English game.

It has been revealed that 40. Mornflake Stadium, Crewe Alexandra.

Division: League Two Opened: 1906 Capacity: 10,109.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was in 1983, which isn’t a high bar, and it has a better owner than it did then.

Industry observers note that I have got a lot of affection for Gresty Road. On a Friday night at the end of September 1983, it was where I saw Micky Quinn score a hat-trick for Stockport County at the home of our bitter rivals.

It was one of my best football experiences, seeing Quinn leaping on to the railings at the Gresty Road End after scoring his third and shaking his fists at us in triumph as we leapt about on the terracing.

If there was footage of the fans’ wild celebrations now, the caption might say ‘limbs’.

Gresty Road is a better stadium now than it was then (which isn’t a high bar) and it has a better owner than it did then. But it can’t be easy living in the shadow of such mighty neighbours.

Industry observers note that 39. SMH Group Stadium, Chesterfield.

Division: League Two Opened: 2010 Capacity: 10,400.

I loved the old ground at Saltergate but when the club moved to the newly introduced stadium and called it the b2net Stadium, it felt as if it had sold its soul.

I used to have a bit of a vendetta against the SMH Group Stadium. Perhaps not a vendetta, but certainly a prejudice.

I loved the old ground at Saltergate but when the club moved to the newly introduced stadium and called it the b2net Stadium, it felt as if it had sold its soul. Since 2009, it has also been called the Proact Stadium and the Technique Stadium.

Sources indicate that but getting to know a club sometimes changes your view of a place. I spent a bit of time there last season when I went to watch Kieron Dyer, who was a coach at the club, and Paul Cook, the manager, at work.

Recent findings suggest that I met the owners, who are local businessmen and clearly have the club’s best interests at heart, and took in a game. Suddenly the SMH Group Stadium had latest life and character and soul breathed into it for me. It’s a club on the up and it’s a club that cares about its fans, and so my prejudice against the SMH Group Stadium is no more.

38. Boundary Park, Oldham Athletic.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 13,186.

Boundary Park is not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

I remember the cold at Boundary Park. I think a lot of people do.

For a long time, I laboured under the misapprehension that it was the highest ground in the Football League when, in fact, that distinction belongs to the Hawthorns.

Recent findings suggest that boundary Park just feels like it should be the highest. It’s not the most beautiful of stadiums but it’s got some grand old character and it’s embedded at the heart of its community.

It just so happens some of my best friends are Oldham fans, too, so I was delighted when they came up from the National League in 2025. It’s a treat to have the ground back in the 92.

Division: League One Opened: 1950 Capacity: 15,036.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park - it was the first away ground I ever went to.

I’ve got a soft spot for Vale Park.

It was the first away ground I ever went to and I still remember the excitement of planning the train journey from Stockport, making it to Burslem and getting a thrill out of the entirely different experience – the extra camaraderie – that being an away fan at another club’s ground brings.

Vale Park felt raw and real to me back then and it got even better on my next visit when, in Stockport’s final year in the Football League before relegation to the National League, Anthony Elding got the winner for County in the 87th minute in front of the away end.

It was beautiful mayhem. County were relegated a few weeks later but I’ll never forget those days at Vale Park.

36. Toughsheet Community Stadium, Bolton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1997 Capacity: 28,018.

This is one of the earliest, and best, of the new generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of Bolton, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury there - and he threatened to have my jaw broken.

When it was the Macron Stadium, one of its several previous incarnations, I interviewed Tyson Fury in a room at the hotel that was part of the Toughsheet Community Stadium in the build-up to his world title fight with Wladimir Klitschko.

After he’d claimed the Klitschkos were part of a devil-worshipping ring, Fury made some rather unpleasant comments about his views on links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

It has been revealed that when the interview was printed, he did not seem best pleased with the results. He said his brother, Substantial Shane, was going to break my jaw ‘completely’ with a straight right hand.

‘See significant Shane there?’ Fury remarked. ‘Have a look at big Shane. He’s 6ft 6in and 25st. He’s going to break (your) jaw completely with one straight right hand. I ain’t going to do it, ‘cos I’ll get in trouble. But the big fella, there – he’ll annihilate (you), won’t he? So Oliver, take a good look at him, because that’s the face you’re going to see before you hit the deck.’.

Fun times. I’ve never found quite the same level of excitement in watching Bolton Wanderers there, although it had some great days in the 2000s when it was called the Reebok and Sam Allardyce was the manager.

It is one of the earliest, and best, of the latest generation of stadiums, and even if it is on the outskirts of the town, its bold design makes it a local landmark.

Division: Championship Opened: 1899 Capacity: 20,899.

Fratton Park has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Since Luton Town's brief sojourn in the Premier League, everyone has become aware of the entrances to their Kenilworth Road ground, through what appears to be the ground floor of a terraced house.

But the old way in to Fratton Park, beneath a half-timbered gable, is even more charming.

One of the old institutions of English football, the stadium has been renovated but has not lost the intensity and the raucousness that makes it such a hostile place to visit for opposing teams.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 29,813.

Portman Road is still a wonderful stadium, a ground at the centre of its community, where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson.

In a recent development, the matchday hospitality of the Cobbolds, the former owners of Ipswich Town, was legendary amongst journalists. I missed out on those days but a visit to Portman Road is still a treat.

It is still a wonderful ground, a ground at the centre of its community, a ground where you can breathe in the legends of Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson, great football men who did great things in their time in charge of the club.

A few years ago, I went to the launch of Kieron Dyer’s autobiography in a suite at the stadium and it was a night that underlined how important the club is to the town.

It is a joy to see that the current hierarchy value the importance of the stadium and have lavished care and money on it. It is one of the great outposts of the English game.

33. Molineux, Wolverhampton Wanderers.

Division: Championship Opened: 1889 Capacity: 31,750.

Molineux is a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

When I first started going to Molineux, it was dominated by a peculiarity.

One of the stands, the John Ireland Stand as it was then, was about 100ft from the touchline, a matter of much mirth for visiting fans.

It has been renamed the Steve Bull Stand now and the pitch has been repositioned so that the modern Molineux is a stadium that makes sense.

It is an arena to be proud of again for Wolves fans, a stadium whose four stands are named after club legends and previous owner and benefactor Sir Jack Hayward, and which takes care to respect its glorious past.

Division: Championship Opened: 1883 Capacity: 21,990.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football, where you can gaze out over the town and its mills.

Turf Moor is a wonderful place to watch football.

Sit in the North Stand, opposite the Bob Lord Stand, and you can gaze out over the town and its mills, which do not look quite as dark and satanic any more, and remember that you are in the traditional northern heartlands of our game here.

I have a friend from Burnley who insists that more people per head wear the jersey of their hometown club in Burnley than in any other football centre in England.

This is a club, after all, that may be bouncing between the Premier League and Championship now but which won the league title in 1921 and 1960 and was once a giant of the game here.

Stoke seems to have been put on a pedestal for thier ability to provide a hostile environment for visiting teams – but Turf Moor can serve up the weather and the atmosphere to run it close.

Recent findings suggest that 31. The Hawthorns, West Bromwich Albion.

Division: Championship Opened: 1900 Capacity: 26,688.

The Hawthorns is the highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, and it is also one of football’s great theatres.

I have seen a few crackers at The Hawthorns.

The 5-5 draw between West Brom and Manchester United in May 2013 that was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last game as a manager is probably top of the list.

I was in the press room there in May 2017 when Chelsea sealed the title under Antonio Conte and the players invaded his press conference to shower him in champagne and generally rough him up. Conte did not look best pleased.

The highest league ground in England, sitting on its perch above the M5, it is also one of football’s great theatres, a ground where the support exudes a love for the game and a warmth that survives the vicissitudes of the club’s fortunes on the pitch.

30. Cledara Abbey Stadium, Cambridge United.

Division: League One Opened: 1932 Capacity: 8,024.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside the Abbey Stadium would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

I made it to the Abbey Stadium for the first time on Latest Year's Day 2025 for the game against Reading.

I walked to the ground down Cut Throat Lane and stood on the terraces at the Newmarket Road End where the singing is at its loudest and where the names and shirts of the celebrated early 1990s team of John Beck, which included Dion Dublin, are painted on the wall at the back of the stand.

Cambridge might be in League One but the noise inside would have put plenty of Premier League grounds to shame.

According to recent reports, 29. Deepdale, Preston North End.

Division: Championship Opened: 1878 Capacity: 23,404.

I love going to Deepdale just for the history. Just to gaze down from the stands and know this is where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

I love going to Deepdale just for the history of the place. Just to gaze down from the stands and know that this was where Tom Finney once played is enough to make it a memorable experience.

And the sense of it being a pilgrimage is only enhanced by the fact that one of the best statues in football sits outside the ground.

Taking its inspiration from the 1956 sports photo of the year, which indicated Finney aquaplaning through a huge puddle at Stamford Bridge, the sculpture, known as The Splash, immortalises Finney outside his hometown club.

It’s a wonderful tribute outside an arena redolent with memories of one of England’s greatest players.

According to recent reports, 28. Kenilworth Road, Luton Town.

Division: League One Opened: 1905 Capacity: 10,265.

Luton will move to a latest stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

The stadium entrance goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses.

In a recent development, the first time I went to Kenilworth Road was 43 years ago. I stood on the open terrace that hosted the away fans for an FA Cup fourth round tie that Manchester United won 2-0.

The most recent time I went was in November 2021, to see Neil Warnock break the record for the most games managed in English football but unable to stop his Middlesbrough team falling to a 3-1 defeat.

Across those decades, the atmosphere at the old stadium has endured. The Main Stand, which is more than a hundred years old, shook that night as Luton took Boro down and the stadium became a bear pit.

Industry observers note that it attained a kind of fame all over again when the club’s return to the top flight recently focused attention on the quirky Oak Road End entrance that goes straight through the middle of a row of terraced houses. Luton will move to a latest stadium at Power Court in the city centre in a few years but Kenilworth Road will be missed.

In a recent development, 27. Etihad Stadium, Manchester City.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2002 Capacity: 61,038.

The Etihad is this high on the list because it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history - even if that all feels a little tainted now.

Sources indicate that I’d probably have Maine Road in the top three in this list if Manchester City still played there. I loved that ground. I loved the benches in the Platt Lane stand, I loved standing on the Kippax, I loved the cantilever Main Stand and the alleyways around the ground and walking across Platt Fields to the game.

But the Etihad isn’t Maine Road. It’s this high on the list because it’s in Manchester and it’s witnessed one of the best teams in English football history playing on its turf, marshalled by one of the game’s great managers – even if all that feels a little tainted by City's guilty verdict in their case with the Premier League, subject to appeal.

City have done their best to breathe personality into it but it’s hard to disguise the fact it’s a characterless, identikit modern stadium.

The corporate denizens of the Tunnel Club, traipsing back to their seats well after the whistle has blown for the start of the second half, don’t help, either.

26. Rodney Parade, Newport County.

Division: League Two Opened: 1877 Capacity: 8,722.

Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play for the FA Cup.

A Cardiff taxi driver once told me that the best fights in Wales happen outside Newport railway station late on Saturday nights. He mentioned he sometimes took a break just to go and watch the action.

Sources indicate that rodney Parade’s a fine place to watch sport, too. Not far from the banks of the River Usk, it’s a modern stadium with remnants of character that come into its own when the giants come to play in the FA Cup.

I was there a few years ago when Manchester City visited in the fifth round and after the game, the way out for fans took them past the open windows of the small changing rooms behind one of the goals where you could hear the celebrations of Pep Guardiola’s team booming out into the South Wales night.

Like the railway station, it’s not a place for the faint-hearted.

Recent findings suggest that 25. Nigel Eady County Ground, Swindon Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1892 Capacity: 15,547.

According to recent reports, my most recent trip to the County Ground was a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley last year. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

There were more than 20 years between my first visit to the County Ground and my most recent, a 0-0 draw with Accrington Stanley in March 2025. It wasn’t the best game but I had the best time.

I’d had a week of being abused on social media by Newcastle fans (which is part of the job and, yes, I agree, I don’t have to read it) and going to Swindon felt like a wonderful breeze blowing on my face.

Sources indicate that for a start, there were more than 7,000 supporters there, for a fourth-tier game which meant nothing to both teams in terms of promotion or relegation. The atmosphere was lively and passionate and the ground has character and warmth, even if one of the ends was closed.

Recent findings suggest that at half-time, I watched a DS Active match between lads with Down Syndrome representing Swindon and Bristol City and it was a joy. It was a joy to see their uncomplicated joy in the beauty of football and the way they celebrated their goals and their skill and the way they looked for their parents in the stands when they scored and the way they supported their team-mates.

The match was a reminder of what it means for a football club to be at the heart of its community. A stadium is about more than just a game.

24. American Express Stadium, Brighton & Hove Albion.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2011 Capacity: 31,876.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

Maybe it is the knowledge of where Brighton & Hove Albion came from to get here that makes a visit to the Amex Stadium such an uplifting thing.

I remember seeing them at the Goldstone Ground, which I loved, but also at the Withdean Stadium, which is a glorified parks pitch inside a small athletics stadium.

When you have commuted to ‘home’ games at Gillingham’s Priestfield Stadium for two years as well, it is little wonder the Amex still feels like the promised land.

Sometimes, just the walk to a stadium is part of what makes it special.

Lots of stadiums are referred to as cathedrals but St James’ Park is the one that fits the description best.

Craven Cottage, home of Fulham, is one of the jewels of English football heritage.

Craven Cottage is one of the jewels of English football heritage, and Fulham’s stadium on the banks of the Thames has achieved the difficult task of modernising the ground without losing its character.

The presence of the Cottage, the most glorious eccentricity remaining in our 92 stadiums, in one corner of the ground, is central to that, of course, and helps to make watching a match there so special.

This is a club that has taken care to preserve its history and value a stadium that is different.

Division: League Two Opened: 1904 Capacity: 8,714.

Exeter City have been owned by their supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, they are a shining example of how successful the model can be.

I was there last year to see Stockport County play and every away fan got a voucher offering a free cup of tea.

It was the summer of 2010 when Exeter City forward Adam Stansfield died of cancer at the age of 31.

‘Stanno’, the father of current Birmingham striker Jay Stansfield, was a hero at the beautiful St James Park stadium, nestled in a nook at the foot of a steep hill and bordered by neat, densely packed terraced streets and a railway cutting.

I drove down there with my elder daughter to look at the tributes to Stansfield and we wandered among the bouquets of flowers and the keepsakes left by heartbroken young fans and the emotional messages that had been left in their thousands on the Significant Bank.

It was impossible not to be moved by the profound emotional connection between a city and its club and as the years have passed, St James Park has come to embody for me everything that a football ground should be: full of character and care and camaraderie and community and passion and pride in what it stands for.

I was there last year to see Stockport play and there was a note next to the away turnstile – a turnstile made in another age at the Albion Works in Patricroft – saying: ‘Hatters Fans: Thank you for travelling 474 miles to support your club today.’.

Every away fan also got a voucher offering a free cup of tea. The club has been owned by its supporters for more than two decades and, despite some recent strife, it is a model of how successful it can be.

It has been revealed that the Big Bank has been extended and is now the biggest terrace in English football. So the locals tell me, anyway. There is a club museum, a stall selling farm produce and a supporters’ club bar with big screens.

Recent findings suggest that they built a newly introduced stand a few years back, too. It’s called the Adam Stansfield Stand.

In a recent development, 3. Hill Dickinson Stadium, Everton.

Division: Premier League Opened: 2025 Capacity: 52,769.

If you are going to move to a fresh ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium.

I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

In a recent development, I loved Goodison Park and I hated the idea of Everton moving from it. I understand, too, the attitude of some Evertonians who feel the identity of the club will be forever twinned with Goodison.

Industry observers note that but if you are going to move to a newly introduced ground, move to somewhere like Hill Dickinson Stadium. I was stunned by how spectacular it is, inside and out, when I went for the first time for the match between Everton and Manchester United in February 2026.

I loved everything about it, from its setting on the banks of Mersey, at the heart of the city’s dock culture, which is such a critical component of Liverpool’s heritage, to its vertiginous stands and its community feel.

It still feels like Everton. It doesn’t feel as if the club has been deracinated by its move, as West Ham have been by the change to the London Stadium. Everton now have a stadium that is one of the city’s great landmarks, the first thing visitors to the city see when they sail in on the cruise ships that arrive in Liverpool from all over the world.

Next to the stadium, there still stands the careworn edifice of Victoria Tower, the famous hexagonal clocktower also known as the Dockers’ Clock, that cruise ship passengers used to set their watches to when they arrived from the USA in the city’s boom times. Everton’s home stands proudly beside it now, a symbol of a latest Merseyside.

Even more than the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Everton's ground is a standard-bearer for the fresh generation of English stadiums.

Division: Premier League Opened: 1884 Capacity: 61,726.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing thanks to fearsome tales about The Kop.

Recent findings suggest that some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't then and it isn’t now.

Growing up in Manchester, Anfield was a place I grew up fearing.

The tales of The Kop and what they would do to you if they heard your accent were fearsome and when I finally plucked up the courage to go and watch Manchester United play there, I bought a ticket among the home fans and did not speak a word for more than two hours.

In a recent development, but that didn’t stop me being in awe of the place when I first visited. I have never been anywhere like it for the passion and the noise it generated.

Yes, maybe its atmosphere has been slightly diluted by the owners' attempts to attract a new, high-yield breed of casual fan but the ferocity of the emotion the place can still muster can be incredibly moving.

The 2005 Champions League semi-final second leg against Chelsea was probably the noisiest and the most spine-tingling I’ve ever witnessed it although the tie against Barcelona, at the same stage of the competition in 2019, is seared on my brain for similar reasons.

A love for a stadium is about memories, too. My first jobs in journalism were on the Daily Post and the Liverpool Echo and I spent many wide-eyed afternoons in the old press box at Anfield and in the press conferences afterwards, listening to Kenny Dalglish and, later, Graeme Souness, two of the best British footballers who have ever lived.

Recent findings suggest that once, on my first visit to the press box, I made the mistake of sitting in Tommy Smith’s seat and was suddenly aware of the hulking presence of the Anfield Iron looming silently above me and a colleague telling me to get up sharpish. I never sat in that seat again.

Some rival fans say the Anfield atmosphere is a myth. It wasn't and it isn’t. Corporate incursions have altered it but it still has the power to make the hairs on the back of your neck stand on end.

1. Edgeley Park, Stockport County.

Division: League One Opened: 1891 Capacity: 10,800.

Sources indicate that I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for Stockport. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

It has been revealed that my family didn’t have any history with Stockport County. I can’t boast a grandfather or an uncle who once played for them. My dad was never much of a football fan and was more likely to ask me ‘How did United get on?’.

But he was from Heaton Chapel and his grandfather made, and lost, a fortune in the hatting industry in the town in the late 19th century, and he was fiercely proud of Stockport Viaduct and its history and he took me to my first game at Edgeley Park on Monday, April 9, 1979.

We sat in Block A of the Main Stand, now the Danny Bergara Stand, and I breathed in the smell of cigar smoke that drifted up from the man in the sheepskin jacket sitting a couple of rows in front of us and thrilled at the noise coming from the terraces opposite and gazed up to my left at the men working away on their typewriters in the press box, men whose faces I recognised because I had seen their photo bylines in the Manchester Evening News.

I have mentioned elsewhere the curious wonder I felt when people who were strangers to me greeted my dad by name as we walked up the steps to our seats.

I didn’t think my dad had ever been to Edgeley Park before but these people knew him anyway because they were from Stockport and he was from Stockport and those moments made me realise for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community. Not for everyone, but for some of us.

And so even if he wasn’t a fan, I still feel connected to my dad every time I use one of my season tickets, that I bought in a row next to the press box, and gaze over at the place we sat that first time.

I am not a proper fan like the supporters who go week in and week out but I love that ground. I am not a member of any London clubs but Edgeley Park is my club and now, just like my dad, I know people when I go.

I feel fortunate, too, that after the club kissed its fair share of frogs, it has one of the best owners across the whole 92.

Edgeley Park was where I realised for the first time that football grounds are places that hold the soul of a community.

It has been revealed that I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

Mark Stott has not just invested in the first team and dragged County back up into the Football League but he has bought a new training ground and lavished a lot of love on upgrading facilities for fans in the Cheadle End.

The Danny Bergara Stand still oozes character, it is still similar to the way I remember it from that first game in 1979 and much of the rest of the stadium has been renovated and improved.

I haven’t been so much in recent seasons because I've been spending my spare weekends trying to complete my 92.

I’m longing to get back. Every fan will know that feeling, the feeling of going home.

Antonio Conte insists he would love ‘before ending my career to take over a club that is already organised’ after years of ‘building value’ from troubled situations like Juventus, Chelsea, Inter and Napoli.

The coach is presently between jobs after walking away from Napoli in two years where he won the Serie A title and the Supercoppa Italiana.

There were reports he could come to Manchester United or even return to his old side Juve, but he is in no rush for his next role.

Speaking to the Cronache di Spogliatoio podcast, Conte did outline his greatest strength, and why he perhaps eager to cast it aside and do something different next time.

“There is one thing I’d love to do before ending my career as a coach, which is to take over a club that is already organised,” remarked Conte.

In a recent development, “It would be like stepping into a Formula 1 car in pole position. It never happened in my career, but evidently that is just the way it goes for me. I always arrived at complicated situations and was fortunate, but also deserve credit, for taking a team back to victory.

“Often, it involved returning them to their history, a dimension that perhaps they had forgotten.”.

It all sounds like the scenario at Manchester United, who have not won the Premier League since 2013, following in the footsteps of other clubs he went through.

“It happened at Juventus, who got back to winning after seven years, Inter hadn’t won the Scudetto for 10, and Chelsea were coming off a disastrous season when I arrived, finishing in 10th place, but then won the Premier League with me.

“The same was true at Napoli, where they had finished 10th, then I arrived and took them to victory.”.

That also means Conte brings with him certain expectations, something he is quick to point out in press conferences from the very start.

Industry observers note that “It is inevitable that when you arrive with a curriculum like this, you are accompanied by big expectations. People and the media expect you to win. I still remember when I arrived at Napoli, a team that finished 10th, a beautiful city, their objective was to qualify for the Champions League.

It has been revealed that “I thought I could just enjoy my work and the city for a while, but the moment I signed, the media completely changed the message. I don’t know how many other coaches would be treated that way.”.

In fairness, Napoli had won the Scudetto the previous season under Luciano Spalletti, then limped to 10th place after going through a series of coaches, but retained much the same team.

When it comes to Inter, Conte also argues he laid the foundations for all those who followed him.

Sources indicate that “I arrived and the Appiano Gentile ground was disastrous, the pitches had big holes in, there was always an alibi from the staff. Inter invested in revamping the pitch, and a month later it was ruined again,” stated the coach.

Industry observers note that “The club spent €120,000 and in those two years, I also asked for them to set up somewhere to sleep. If you look at the Inter training ground today, it is a gem.

“There are many clubs where there is a before me, and an after me, and those who come later find this.”.

Conte also discussed the player sales that sides like Inter made thanks to his development of certain players.

“I become an investment for clubs that pays off. We signed Romelu Lukaku and Achraf Hakimi, then sold them on for €120m to Chelsea and €70m to PSG. I added value to the squad.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change.
  • "It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a newly introduced study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Recent findings suggest that emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.".

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

Industry observers note that the study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sources indicate that A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters mentioned. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%.".

It has been revealed that it is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

Sources indicate that and even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, as of 10:16 GMT, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has journeyed one light-day, or 25.9 billion kilometres, from Earth — farther than any human-made object has gone before. At this distance, signals from Earth’s surface travelling at light speed will take a full 24 hours to reach the craft. The trailblazing probe is expected to lose communications with Earth in 2029, when its plutonium power finally dies. But that time might not signal the end of Voyager 1’s contributions — the craft carries a golden record engraved with sights and sounds from Earth, an interspecies message for any aliens who might encounter it as it continues its journey.

A device that stimulates the brain with flickering light and rhythmic clicking sounds has failed to slow memory loss in people with Alzheimer’s disease. The Spectris AD headset is designed to induce brain activity called gamma waves, which have been linked to increased attention and memory. The results of a long-anticipated clinical trial highlighted that participants who used the device did not show robust improvements in their cognitive function after a year of treatment compared with those assigned to a sham treatment. The results were reported at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease meeting on 16 November.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has announced that the United States has lost its measles elimination status amid an outbreak that’s caused more than 5,700 infections and 10 deaths this year. The US had eliminated measles in 2000 after an intensive vaccination campaign. But declining vaccination rates in the past few years have left pockets of the population vulnerable to infection. “We’ve taken an enormous step back in public health,” says virologist Paul Offit. Measles has also been re-established in Mexico and Bolivia, PAHO announced.

Source: International Vaccine Access Center, Johns Hopkins University.

Sources indicate that consumer tests that promise to reveal the full range of microbes living in your gut are taking off — but their results can vary widely. “This is an industry that’s running wild,” indicates genomicist Jacques Ravel, who co-authored a study that tested several providers. With regard to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”. But it’s hard to set those standards, writes journalist Amber Dance, who sent off her own stool to investigate the field. Part of the problem is that “there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample”, she says.

It has been revealed that the proportion of reviewers at Nature who are early-career researchers. Increasing it would benefit all researchers and science as a whole, argues a Nature editorial. (Nature | 6 min read).

Amid the tedium of investigating potentially fraudulent papers, “there is some light relief, thanks to some hilarious phrases used by authors seeking to avoid detection by plagiarism checkers”, writes research-integrity sleuth Dorothy Bishop. Bishop and Nature’s careers team have compiled a quiz to test your ability to match ‘tortured phrases’ — those that replace common words with synonyms in an attempt to skirt past plagiarism-detection software — with their original text.

From the Bering Strait to Doggerland, much of human history occurred in places that are now underwater, covered by the sea-level rise that occurs after ice ages. Geographer Jerome Dobson has dubbed this drowned land ‘Aquaterra’. It’s the site of many discoveries — such as Blinkerwall in the Baltic Sea, one of Europe’s oldest and largest Stone Age structures — and possibly many more to come. It also offers an interesting thought experiment: if we continue to drive global warming, what might future archaeologists make of our inundated world?

Italy international Gianluigi Donnarumma received criticism lately, but Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca and former goalkeeper Joe Hart rushed to his defence.

The shot-stopper was guilty of a few howlers for the Azzurri in the Nations League, most notably in the 3-1 victory over France, but also made a series of big saves over the two matches.

He will be suspended for the next Italy match in 2027, although that will not be in the Nations League after finishing third in the group behind France and Belgium.

“He has been good,” assured Manchester City coach Maresca with regards to Donnarumma.

Industry observers note that “I think with the international team, he made a mistake in the build-up. But in Italy he was the man of the match in the game, he made many good saves.

“We made some mistakes in the last games. Gigi was part of that. He is aware. Hopefully he’s not going to make any more mistakes. He is going to start against Fulham.”.

Former Manchester City, Torino and England goalkeeper Hart has also used his column on the official City website to heap praise upon the Italian, who only recently won the Champions League at Paris Saint-Germain.

Donnarumma also won the Yashin Trophy, the goalkeeper’s equivalent of the Ballon d’Or, twice.

It has been revealed that “I think some of Gianluigi’s performances were breathtaking, absolutely astonishing. He’s the captain of Italy. Simply put, he’s at the top table of goalkeepers,” wrote Hart.

“I think he’s proven his quality and his ability on numerous occasions since joining City. Yes he’s not had the best couple of months but that’s the life of a goalkeeper. He’ll have experienced it before. He’ll experience it again. We shouldn’t forget all the brilliant stuff he does for the team.”.

Hart praised Donnarumma’s role in the locker room too, noting he is “a really beautiful human being” and “renowned for his hugs.”.

#71745. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1002 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).
  • The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.
  • Recent findings suggest that "In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

Recent findings suggest that "In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late.".

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health challenges.

All B vitamins play an key role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That noted, even some people in industrialized nations lack vital micronutrients in their nutrition.

Industry observers note that one study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

Sources indicate that about one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

According to recent reports, the cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Recent findings suggest that malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research indicates that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

It has been revealed that the DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data indicates that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a proposal to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults.".

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

In a recent development, the nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," noted Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

Sources indicate that but even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki went from being serenaded with a chorus of “world’s No 1” to making a bizarre blunder that denied Unai Emery’s side a third successive Premier League victory.

The Villa manager, however, preferred to focus on a string of crucial saves from Suzuki rather than the uncharacteristic mistake that allowed Fulham to collect a deserved point.

It all went wrong for the hosts just after the hour mark in a match where Fulham provided more than a few scares before finding the net in unexpected fashion.

Recent findings suggest that alex Iwobi, who had been denied superbly by a Suzuki save just moments earlier, swung in a corner. It was right on top of the Villa goalkeeper, who tried to keep it out but only succeeded in fumbling it over the line. A frantic attempt to gather the ball was in vain and goal-line technology confirmed the goal stood.

Suzuki appeared to have been put off by the presence of Fulham’s Shea Charles, but Emery refused to single out the player for criticism.

According to recent reports, “I prefer to speak about the saves that he made,” the Villa manager remarked. “This is part of football. I think he played fantastically and he is doing a lot of saves so he can make one mistake. It is part of football. We can be mature about this.

“I still want to see consistency. Over the last five Premier League matches, we are winning three and drawing two. It’s not bad but with our poor start it’s not enough.

According to recent reports, “We have to change our mind swiftly for Tuesday against Barcelona. We want to test ourselves at this level.”.

In a recent development, villa go to the Nou Camp with a 100 per cent Champions League record to their name this season. But they will need to improve on Saturday evening’s performance to get a result in Spain.

As well as Suzuki’s error, a 14th-minute penalty miss from John McGinn also proved costly.

It has been revealed that it was awarded after Leon Goretzka, making his full league debut for Villa, saw his header hit Sander Berge’s raised hand. Nobody appealed at the time but referee Sam Barrott was sent to the touchline monitor by VAR to review the incident and gave the spot-kick.

It has been revealed that mcGinn’s attempt, however, hit the crossbar and the chance to take an early lead went begging. The Villa captain seemed a strange choice to take the spot-kick as he has only ever scored one career penalty, but Emery defended the choice, saying: “We analysed the penalty takers in the squad and it was McGinn here.”.

Nicolas Jackson was on hand to ease Villa’s nerves before the break, though. the Villa manager had said before the game that the striker’s goalscoring capability meant he was capable of matching the likes of Harry Kane. His assessment was backed up by Jackson scoring the opening goal, after 40 minutes, which summed up the striker in one moment of pure power combined with agility.

Collecting Johan Manzambi’s superbly weighted pass, Jackson forced his way past two defenders before sliding in the goal that put Villa ahead.

Emery’s touchline celebrations stated it all as the Senegal forward continues to flourish under the man who knew how to get the best out of him at Villarreal.

Suzuki has also flourished under Emery and he kept Villa in the game with some superb saves.

Recent findings suggest that when Antonee Robinson crossed for Gonzalo Garcia, his step over allowed Oscar Bobb in for what looked like his second goal in successive games. But Suzuki pulled off a stunning fingertip save. That had Villa supporters singing: “Zion Suzuki, the world’s No 1”.

In a recent development, robinson put in another cross and Suzuki got a touch that was enough to make Garcia put his shot wide. Villa were living dangerously and the Japanese goalkeeper made another outstanding stop to keep out Iwobi’s header. But then it all went wrong for Suzuki when he fumbled Iwobi’s corner.

That allowed Fulham’s recent revival under manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, to continue – they now have seven points from their past three games.

Sources indicate that “We spoke at half-time about what we had to do,” Arbeloa noted. “If you want to win a game you have to fight and I think we have to believe in our way, we’ve shown we can beat anyone in the way that we play but we have to be aggressive.

“We created so many chances and at the end it’s one point in a difficult stadium. I’m so happy with the second half because of the way we played, this is the team that we want to be.”.

Zion Suzuki had significant gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”.

According to recent reports, emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”.

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

It has been revealed that villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”.

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa stated. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

Sources indicate that “They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”.

Sources indicate that in the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Woltemade only joined Juventus on loan from Newcastle United, but it’s reported they want to make it permanent, selling Francisco Conceicao to raise the necessary funds.

The German centre-forward was a very late signing to Serie A, arriving on deadline day on a 12-month loan for €3.6m, and not including any option to make it permanent.

He has scored four goals with two assists in 13 appearances between Serie A and the Europa League, working well on his own, or in a partnership with Randal Kolo Muani.

According to La Gazzetta dello Sport, the 24-year-old has impressed Juventus directors enough that they are hatching a blueprint to buy him outright at the end of the season.

That will require some strong negotiation, considering Newcastle United paid a massive €75m to buy him from VfB Stuttgart in the summer of 2025.

He did not live up to those expectations, finding the net 11 times with six assists in 53 games for the Premier League club.

It would be a significant expense for Juve, who are hoping to ask for an extended loan and option to buy in June 2028 for a lower fee.

They can also raise funds by selling Francisco Conceicao, who would generate a profit for anything over €40m.

It could even be possible to send the Portugal international to Newcastle United as part of any potential swap deal with Woltemade.

Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S.
  • Homo erectus is already one of humans’ most extraordinary ancient relatives.
  • Sources indicate that did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Homo erectus might have also lived in rainforests — previously thought to be a habitat in which only modern humans could have thrived.Credit: S. Entressangle/E. Daynes/SPL.

Homo erectus is already one of humans’ most extraordinary ancient relatives. The substantial-brained, tool-wielding species emerged two million years ago in Africa and expanded across Eurasia, before vanishing around 100,000 years ago in Java, Indonesia.

Sources indicate that did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts.

Did Homo erectus and Denisovans mate? Tooth proteins hint at ancient trysts.

Industry observers note that researchers have now added another feather to the hominin’s cap. A pair of studies analysing fossil teeth1,2, which were published in Nature on 18 November, suggest that H. erectus thrived in dense rainforests in southern China as recently as 180,000 years ago.

Researchers had thought that H. erectus was limited to savannahs and open woodlands, notes Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia, and a co-author of both studies.

Recent findings suggest that “Never, ever have we seen them in rainforests,” she adds. “This is a really big deal, because we thought Homo sapiens were the only species that had the skill set to survive in really challenging rainforest environments.”.

The earliest H. erectus fossils, from eastern Africa, are 1.9 million years old. But the svelte, upright-walking and running hominins wasted little time, reaching western Asia and present-day China some 200,000 years later and modern Java, using land bridges, not long after. The last-known H. erectus remains, from central Java, date to roughly 110,000 years ago3.

Limestone caves in Guangxi province, southern China, contained more than 10,000 fossil teeth.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University).

According to recent reports, while looking for fossils from a three-metre-tall great ape called Gigantopithecus, Westaway and her colleagues identified a pair of limestone caves in Guangxi province in southern China. There, they discovered more than 10,000 fossil teeth from animals such as orangutans (Pongo spp.), monkeys and wild boar (Sus spp.), as well as 9 from hominins. The researchers estimate that the hominins lived between 184,000 and 324,000 years ago, according to dating of both fossils and the surrounding sediments using various methods.

Recent findings suggest that eight of the hominin teeth resembled those of H. erectus in their shape, a designation that was confirmed by analysing the sequences of proteins preserved in the dental enamel of four specimens, says co-author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen.

The tooth enamel was analysed and its proteins sequenced.Credit: Kira Westaway (Macquarie University).

According to recent reports, the ninth lacked the shape and protein signature of H. erectus teeth, says Welker, and it also didn’t resemble those of H. sapiens or Neanderthals (Homo neanderthalensis). Denisovans — enigmatic ancient humans first discovered in southern Siberia and now linked to diverse fossils from China and elsewhere in Asia — are a possibility, but the evidence is circumstantial, says Welker. “Every label we put on that ninth tooth is a little bit of speculation.”.

The multitude of animal teeth was probably accumulated by a scavenger such as a porcupine. The presence of fossils from species such as muntjac deer (Muntiacus muntjac), leopards and orangutans hints at a rainforest environment.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.
  • "Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

Industry observers note that "These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation.".

Industry observers note that yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects at the moment in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," remarked Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, remarked Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions.".

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," noted Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Industry observers note that australia must commit to "substantial newly introduced funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

Industry observers note that A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," stated Houlie.
