  • At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.
  • Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

In a recent development, and then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes stated after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

In a recent development, he had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

NO MISTAKE THIS TIME 💪 Bruno Fernandes gets United back in it after a penalty retake 😤 https://t.co/uQdkNs0lXo.

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

Recent findings suggest that from being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

IT'S 2-2! 💥 Cunha levels it up for United! 🔴🇧🇷 https://t.co/q60oQUoat1.

At that point, the momentum was firmly in United’s favour and three minutes later they were in front. It is a source of bemusement among fans that Shea Lacey has not had more game-time considering how poor some senior players have been. And his arrival as a substitute made a big difference.

It has been revealed that it was Lacey who speared an inch-perfect pass into Cunha, who turned sharply before drilling a stunning finish in off the near post. Cue bedlam.

It has been revealed that MAN UNITED HAVE TURNED IT AROUND!!! 🔴🔥 From 2-0 down, to 3-2 up at Old Trafford 🤩 https://t.co/ATD8wDlc1e.

Sources indicate that cunha was booked for taking off his shirt as he crowd-surfed bear-chested among the fans and was then sent off minutes later after a poor challenge. A fittingly chaotic end to a crazy night for the match-winner.

The difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

Sources indicate that on the pitch, United were all over the place. Carrick had dropped Lisandro Martínez after his red card against Chelsea but his replacement Ayden Heaven was at fault for the first goal after getting sucked in and failing to check his shoulder. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

Malen continued his rich scoring vein from the penalty spot.

Industry observers note that at that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

Recent findings suggest that “It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

According to recent reports, “I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”.

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”.

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

In a recent development, “Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he noted.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”.

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

In a recent development, “It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was crucial to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”.

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”.

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

Industry observers note that “It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”.

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, substantial character, big fight.”.

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”.

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we demonstrated what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”.

“Great credit to Michael Carrick because they were down and out at half-time. They were everywhere in that first-half, and he had to change and tweak things,” Alan Shearer stated after the final whistle.

“I stated what can he do, I didn’t know where he would start, and he must have started in the dressing room, and pointing at a few people telling them to be brave and courageous and move the ball quicker, and run in behind and they did all those things in the second half and got their reward by getting their win.”.

Thousands of green and gold balloons – a nod to the club’s original colours as Newton Heath – are set to be released from the Stretford End when the Champions League music plays out ahead of kick-off.

There had been aims to bring a banner into the stadium bearing the words: “No latest stadium, we want new owners” but that was blocked, apparently on the grounds of Uefa’s inability to sanction it in time.

Happy Tuesday and thanks for tuning in to tonight’s coverage of Manchester United against Roma.

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. This has been coupled with dismal performances in the Premier League, most recently a 2-0 defeat at the hands of Chelsea, where Lisandro Martínez was sent off for two ridiculous fouls.

Lisandro Martinez is shown a second yellow card following a VAR review 🟥 Watch live on TNT Sports and HBO Max ➡️https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/VLcAMNdqgZ.

Sources indicate that all in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. They got off to a slow start in Europe, drawing with Fernebahce in their opening match but coming agonisingly close to stunning Real Madrid on matchday two at home. They went 3-1 up before three late goals snatched victory for Madrid.

Sources indicate that they bounced back with a convincing 4-0 win over Slovan Bratislava and their domestic campaign is off to an incredibly promising start. They are currently unbeaten in Serie A with seven wins and three draws. They sit third and are the highest scoring side, with 28 goals from their 10 games. Free-flowing though their attack is, there a certainly defensive frailties there to exploit as they conceded three in a six-goal thriller against Napoli, as well as two in both matches against Cagliari and Udinese.

According to recent reports, it has been 19 years since Carrick was part of a United side that thrashed Roma 7-1 at Old Trafford, with the midfielder scoring two. Tonight he faces that same opponent with his job hanging by a thread and it remains to be seen if his team can produce any semblance of that spark to turn the tide. Napoli are back in Serie A action on Saturday evening following the recent international break, and pre-match reports suggest that Kevin De Bruyne will not be included in Massimiliano Allegri’s starting line-up.

Napoli return to league action in desperate need of results after a disappointing start to the campaign that has left them in 10th place on 15 points after 11 matches. They are already 14 points shy of the league leaders and nine points off the Champions League spots.

They won just one of their four league games heading into the international break, albeit in a tough run of fixtures that included draws against Roma and Lazio and a defeat against Juventus.

Ignacio abate, meanwhile, has called for consistency from Torino after winning three games in a row in October, before picking up just one point from their next three heading into the international break.

The visitors are just one point and one position behind Napoli on Saturday morning and will be eyeing an opportunity to leapfrog their opponents into the top half of the Serie A table.

Earlier this week, it was confirmed that goalkeeper Alex Meret will be out for the remainder of the year and beyond with a fractured vertebra in his back, which means that Vanja Milinkovic-Savic is set to start against his former club.

According to Sky Sport Italia, De Bruyne, who has been linked with a January move away from Napoli, is expected to start from the bench. Scott McTominay, Billy Gilmour and Andre-Frank Zambo Anguissa are likely to start in midfield instead.

It could also be a 3-5-2 for Napoli this evening, with Antonio Vergara in contention to partner Rasmus Hojlund in attack.

Napoli (3-5-2): Milinkovic-Savic; Beukema, Rrahmani, Marin; Politano, Anguissa, Gilmour, McTominay, Spinazzola; Vergara, Hojlund.

Torino (3-5-2): Perri; Coco, Ismajli, Comuzzo; Belghali, Casadei, Mandragora, Braganca, Cacciamani; Adams, Simeone.

Breaking: Neuer injury gives Urbig chance to shape Bayern and Germany future

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that getting playing time is crucial to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country .
  • Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception.
  • But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that getting playing time is crucial to the development of any professional footballer – especially if your aspiration is to become the first-choice goalkeeper for your country . For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can.".

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

Sources indicate that the match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment.".

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

This article was adapted from German.

“With him, we’re in a dilemma: he has an illness that isn’t easily curable, but which can be managed reasonably well with medication," he said.

“But whether he’ll ever regain the performance level he once had… For now, he’s still getting paid. But imagine if FC Bayern were to question his contract now and say: ‘What he’s capable of now isn’t what’s stipulated in the contract’.”.

Bayern board member Rummenigge has now given his thoughts on Musiala's condition. He noted that the club needs to talk to the 23-year-old as he isn't justifying his lofty salary, believed to be £370,000-per-week.

“(Musiala) has a health-related glitch. It's also well known that he has a contract involving very substantial sums of money. As a club, we have to consider how to deal with that situation. I think that's responsible and perfectly normal.

“What we know unfortunately suggests it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he has often shown here in this stadium.

“[We need to] talk to the player, to the family and, above all, to the agency, because, with all due respect, those sums are then no longer feasible.

A third wrote: "What a terrible and disgusting statement to put out," while a fourth stated: "'What a vile way to treat a player.".

Bayern manager Kompany has defended Musiala amid criticism Hoeness and Rummenigge's comments. He noted, per Goal:.

“He has a very clear role at this club. A coach has to be the one who believes in the players. If we manage that, everyone wins.

According to recent reports, “If Jamal rediscovers his form and his level, then Bayern Munich win. So do the fans and, I think, German football too. Because he’s a special player. That’s my role. If a coach says or does something else, then that’s a problem, in my personal view.

According to recent reports, “You can’t expect our star players to make the difference immediately. If Lucho Diaz plays 20 minutes next week, we can’t expect him to decide the game straight away. That’s not realistic. Jamal Musiala is in the process of being reintegrated, and Lucho will soon begin his reintegration too.

"Right now, it’s about other players. At some point, those players will be 100 per cent fit to play again, and then we’ll enjoy that again too.”.

New Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has been tipped to make Fulham defender Antonee Robinson his very first signing at Old Trafford.

That is according to a report from Football Insider, which claims that the left-back has been on the radar of the Red Devils for quite some time and continues to be high on their list of transfer targets.

Having worked closely with the 29-year-old during his tenure in charge of the United States national team, including all four matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, Pochettino is reportedly eager to reunite with the defender.

Speaking on Football Insider’s Transfer Insider podcast, transfer correspondent Pete O’Rourke explained why Robinson sits right at the top of Pochettino’s winter shortlist:.

In a recent development, “Yeah, of course, there’ll always be speculation about which players Mauricio Pochettino could look to bring in. Like you said, Antonee Robinson has been a long-term target for United and obviously United do have problems at left back as well.

“And with Luke Shaw’s contract coming up to expire in the summer as well, they’re going to have to do something in that area to try and improve this team. Robinson is somebody they have been looking at for a while, and if Pochettino wants to recruit some former players, he will be high on that list for him I’m sure.”.

Left-back has become an urgent priority for Manchester United’s recruitment team.

With Luke Shaw’s contract set to expire at the end of the season and ongoing fitness concerns continuing to disrupt the squad’s defensive stability, Pochettino requires an athletic, durable full-back capable of executing his high-pressing, overlapping system from day one.

Diogo Dalot has also failed to impress this season, with his performances coming under criticism both at left-back and right-back.

Robinson, who has already made over 220 senior appearances for Fulham and ranks among the Premier League’s most relentless runners, fits that profile seamlessly.

United’s admiration for the Milton Keynes-born American is not new.

Having previously registered a remarkable 10-assist Premier League campaign in 2024/25, Robinson has remained firmly on Old Trafford’s radar.

With Fulham tying him down until June 2028, and rival clubs such as Liverpool, Chelsea, and Newcastle United also monitoring his situation, Pochettino’s personal relationship with Robinson could prove decisive if United launch a formal bid worth £25 million or more in January.

  • Baldini shared his thoughts on Milan’s cohort of young Italian talents in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport, published on Saturday.
  • The Azzurrini head coach notes that he is impressed with the development and maturity that Cisse has shown over the last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Italy U21s head coach Silvio Baldini says that he has spoken to Francesco Camarda ‘like father-to-son’ and has tipped both Alphadjo Cisse and Davide Bartesaghi to reach the highest heights in the professional game: ‘If I were the coach of any Serie A club, I would take him with me’.

Baldini shared his thoughts on Milan’s cohort of young Italian talents in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport, published on Saturday.

The Azzurrini head coach notes that he is impressed with the development and maturity that Cisse has shown over the last year.

It has been a rapid rise to the top for the Rossoneri winger, who was playing in Serie B with Catanzaro six months ago, has already been fast-tracked through the Italy U21 side and was called up to the senior national side by Roberto Mancini earlier this month.

“Compared to a year ago, I see a completely different guy, stronger, more mature and more prepared with a lot more self-esteem,” Baldini told La Gazzetta dello Sport. “He has Milan to thank for taking him from Catanzaro in Serie B, believing in him and giving him an opportunity to play consistently. If he moves up to the national team and does well, even better.”.

Baldini credited Milan with scouting and developing Cisse, but La Gazzetta dello Sport suggested that it is Baldini who discovered that Cisse could be equally as effective through the middle as he is off the wing.

Recent findings suggest that A humble Baldini shrugged off those suggestions: “After analysing the training sessions, there were lots of situations where he managed to score by attacking space from depth. If he can do it off the left and right flanks, it means he can do it from the centre as well.

It has been revealed that “But still, the credit goes to the staff who had this insight, who understood that Cisse could be useful to our game blueprint in that role. I try to be honest and meritocratic in my decisions.”.

Recent findings suggest that baldini was then asked for his thoughts on Camarda. Tipped for greatness from the age of 15 onwards, some feel that the now-18-year-old has stalled in his development and that he has had a lack of opportunities in the Milan first-team.

Recent findings suggest that “I can only talk about the things that we do together,” noted Baldini. “I spoke to him at length, dedicated some time to him, had him explain his concerns, his fear of not being able to express himself in the way that he would like.

Recent findings suggest that “I responded by telling him stories about myself, my life and how I got out of it. A conversation that was less coach-to-player and more father-to-son, or rather a grandson as he could be for me!

“I try to help him understand what I see, I watch a lot of his small movements. He’s a clever boy who shouldn’t become obsessed with scoring, but should play football to enjoy it, have fun. If it becomes more of a test, then you start to get worried, and if it worries you, you won’t enjoy it and won’t perform at your best.”.

Baldini was asked if he has or if he would advise Camarda to make a move away from Milan to find that enjoyment he mentioned.

“I won’t intervene on that,” he said. There are clubs, agents, families, they know what’s best for him. Let’s remember that he’s 18, he plays for Milan and with the Italy U21s and he also came with me to play two games for the senior national team. Of course, the more he plays the better it is for Milan and for everyone.

It has been revealed that “We’re talking about a great player, a champion for me, who needs to finish his development. He’s still growing, he already finds the goal very well and sacrifices himself for his team.”.

Does Baldini think that Cisse and Camarda could be the future of the Italy national team’s attack?

According to recent reports, “For me, yes, I see them as regulars for the national team. And they have the time to earn it and prove it on the pitch. They have the characteristics to do it. I think Alpha is doing really well with his decisions, Amorim has done well to get the best out of him.”.

Baldini is also a fan of one of Milan’s other young Italian talents, Davide Bartesaghi.

According to recent reports, “Davide is one of the best players I’ve coached in that position for many years,” remarked Baldini. “He’s very good, very professional, very mature. He’s an introverted character but still open, and that’s not a contradiction. He has enormous potential and he shows it every time he’s with us. If I were coach of any Serie A club, I would have him with me.

“Bartesaghi is a luxury for the U21s. He plates with heart, passion, intelligence and has high-level technical, physical and running skills. He can play in all positions on the wing. For me, if he starts 50m away from goal, he performs at his best.”.

Baldini’s interview ended with a massive statement of intent, referring back to a promise he made in an interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport earlier this season.

“It’s a divine gift to be in this role. Kids and family are the most precious things I have. Choosing who to send to the stands is always the hardest part.

According to recent reports, “I said that I wanted to win the European Championship and the Olympics. We’ll work twice as hard to try for that.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that from the electric Kylian Mbappe to the dazzling Lamine Yamal, some of the very best players on the planet at the moment ply their trade in the Spanish top-flight. La Liga is home to incredibly talented superstars and even some of the front-runners for the 2027 Ballon d'Or.

While there often appears to be more money floating about elsewhere, like in the Saudi Pro League and the Premier League, the top clubs in Spain aren't shy about handing out lucrative contracts to attract and retain world-class talent either.

Sources indicate that with Real Madrid and Barcelona players at the forefront of this list, there can be little surprise that the purse strings are often loosened as the biggest stars are tied down to extremely lucrative deals. With that in mind, below is a list of the 21 highest-paid players in La Liga right now.

Top 21 Highest-Paid La Liga Players (21-11).

When at his best, Rodrygo is among the best wingers in the world. He was just 18 when he turned up at Real Madrid, having established himself as the next major talent to emerge at Santos. Since then, the Brazilian has won three La Liga titles and the Champions League twice.

Recent findings suggest that although he might play second fiddle to the likes of Mbappe and Vinicius Junior (more on those two later), Rodrygo is still among the best-paid players in Spain, earning a hefty £271,200 p/w. Sadly, he suffered a torn ACL in March 2026 and might not play again until 2027.

Sources indicate that when he was just about saving Leeds United from relegation in 2022, few would have thought Raphinha was destined to prove himself as one of Barcelona's most key players in the coming seasons. But that's exactly what he has done in Spain.

In a recent development, the brilliant Brazilian can play across any of the front three attacking positions and works incredibly hard for the team, while still delivering moments of magic. This has seen him win three Spanish league titles, and he was even named La Liga Player of the Season in 2024/25. As such, it's more than fair that he is so well-paid.

In a team full of superstar midfielders, Federico Valverde has endeared himself to the Bernabeu faithful through his hard-working performances and his willingness to play anywhere asked of him. That's not to suggest he lacks talent, far from it, as he's now regarded as one of the best midfielders in the league.

Sources indicate that the 28-year-old is well compensated for his efforts, too; walking away with close to £300,000 p/w. For a while, he was among the most underrated names in world football, but his club always recognised his value, and that's well reflected by his handsome wages.

A rare non-Barcelona or Madrid star in this list, Nico Williams has been rewarded for his loyalty to Athletic Club. In 2025, amid strong links to the likes of Barcelona and Arsenal, he committed his future to the club, signing a mammoth 10-year contract worth £279,660 p/w.

For a player on such significant wages, he doesn't always deliver as many goals or assists as some would expect, but he's still only 24 and could yet grow to become a little more consistent. Even so, when he's on it, he's amongst the best in the world. This was clear at Euro 2024, with Williams delivering a serious electric performance as Spain won the tournament.

According to recent reports, aurelien Tchouameni has been one of the first names on the teamsheet for Real Madrid since signing for the club in a €100 million move from Monaco in 2022. Los Blancos beat the likes of Liverpool to his signature.

It has been revealed that following Toni Kroos' retirement and Luka Modric's departure, Tchouameni has only become more important for the Spanish giants. In the summer of 2026, Man Utd are believed to have made a 'very aggressive move' to sign the Frenchman, but Real Madrid didn't have any intention of letting him go.

A few months later, he penned a six-year contract worth a huge £305,039-per-week, making him one of La Liga's highest-paid players.

Only the second player in the top 10 not to play for either Real Madrid or Barcelona. The Atletico Madrid icon had significant shoes to fill when he was chosen to replace long-standing loanee Courtois in 2014. In the decade that followed, Jan Oblak demonstrated himself to be one of the best number ones on the planet.

Recent findings suggest that interest in his services was commonplace. Despite that, Oblak stayed loyal to Diego Simeone and has been financially rewarded in return, now earning more than Courtois. Now 33, it will be interesting to see if Atletico offer him quite such a massive salary when it comes time to renew in 2028.

Sources indicate that this figure is bound to increase in the years to come. In just three seasons in the Spanish capital, Jude Bellingham has established himself as arguably the most crucial player in Los Blancos' superhero-like squad. It has been revealed that mbappe's arrival meant that the 23-year-old fell a little out of the limelight, but his progress has also been hampered by a pesky shoulder injury which required surgery. Madrid will be relieved to have him tied down on a major wage until 2029.

It has been revealed that lamine Yamal has risen to be seen as one of the best players in world football and a strong contender to lift the 2027 Ballon d'Or at the age of just 19. The youngster has always been compared to Barcelona great Lionel Messi, but came out on top as Spain beat Argentina in the 2026 World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that what's more, Yamal is certainly being more handsomely rewarded than Messi was as a teenager, with the Spain international putting pen to paper on a newly introduced deal at the end of the 2024/25 season. He now rakes in £372,880 every week, a wage proportionate to his outstanding talent.

After starring for Spain in their second World Cup triumph this summer, Rodri emerged as a target for both Barcelona and Real Madrid. He soon made a decision to join the Catalans and follow in the footsteps of one of his idols, Sergio Busquets.

Barca agreed on a £65 million deal with Manchester City to bring the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner to Camp Nou. He penned a mammoth deal worth £440,588-per-week, making him the third highest-paid player in La Liga and the highest earner in Hansi Flick's squad.

In the case of Vinicius Jr, the Brazilian felt he deserved a much bigger contract, and he was finally convinced Real Madrid of that as well. After months of negotiations, and with Arsenal lurking in the background, Los Blancos upped their offer and the winger put pen to paper in August 2026 on a deal worth more than £500,000 p/w.

According to recent reports, vini is certainly one of the best players in the world currently and has scored in two Champions League finals, becoming one of Los Blancos' most crucial attacking threats. With that in mind, it's no surprise he wanted better terms.

Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious.
  • But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.
  • This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men.".

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

It has been revealed that "I do think this is nonsense," claims Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

Recent findings suggest that in the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people.".

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

It has been revealed that the Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," notes Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued.".

According to recent reports, on October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The concern of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Industry observers note that germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi noted. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity.".

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

Roy Keane Names Best Football Manager Ever - Snubs Sir Alex Ferguson and Pep Guardiola

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ian Wright, Jamie Carragher and Roy Keane have all named their picks for the greatest football manager of all time - but they disagreed, with all three choosing someone different.
  • Sources indicate that of course, there are many different components that make a great manager.
  • According to recent reports, most of The Overlap panel have now had their say on the debate, with Gary Neville and Jill Scott also revealing their choices, alongside some of the show's producers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ian Wright, Jamie Carragher and Roy Keane have all named their picks for the greatest football manager of all time - but they disagreed, with all three choosing someone different. The latter, meanwhile, sensationally snubbed both Pep Guardiola and the man behind much of his success at Manchester United, Sir Alex Ferguson.

Sources indicate that of course, there are many different components that make a great manager. Some are serial winners, like the two just mentioned, whether through their tactical nous or ability to build successful teams over the long haul. Others, meanwhile, have the personality and charisma to make football transcend the game itself, much like Liverpool greats Bill Shankly and Jurgen Klopp.

According to recent reports, most of The Overlap panel have now had their say on the debate, with Gary Neville and Jill Scott also revealing their choices, alongside some of the show's producers. Interestingly, not a single legendary international manager made the cut, with the likes of Spain's Vicente Del Bosque overlooked.

Wrighty was in no doubt when naming Shankly as the greatest manager in football history, pointing to what the iconic Liverpool boss did for the city as his main reason.

The Scot's trophy cabinet may not have been as glittering as some of his contemporaries', having led the Reds to a First Division title, their historic first FA Cup and a UEFA Cup.

It has been revealed that however, his greatest achievement was laying the foundations for a club that would go on to become the most successful in English football. Liverpool's continued success today is, in many ways, still a testament to Shankly's transformative tenure back in the 1960s.

Carragher, meanwhile, found the question a little harder to answer. After name-checking AC Milan greats Fabio Capello and Arrigo Sacchi, he eventually settled on Pep Guardiola, arguing that the Barcelona side of the early 2010s was the greatest team he had ever seen.

Guardiola's trophy cabinet boasts six Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns, although his Manchester City tenure has since come under greater scrutiny following the club's historic 115 charges guilty verdict.

While Neville stuck to his loyalties and named Ferguson as his greatest manager of all time, Keane went against the Man United grain by instead hailing Brian Clough, despite winning 17 major honours under the former, including seven league titles and a Champions League.

Clough's managerial style combined intense psychological man-management, simple, pass-and-move football and strict personal discipline.

It was perhaps his no-nonsense attitude that endeared him most to Keano, while his success came in an era before money made the world go round in football.

He won top-flight titles with both Derby County and Nottingham Forest, while also guiding the latter to back-to-back European Cups. His ability to build a lasting dynasty clearly hasn't been lost on Keano, who played under Clough at the City Ground for three years after joining Forest from Cobh Ramblers in the summer of 1990 for just £47,000.
